best_for: Students, hobbyists, open-source contributors and small teams of up to five who build .NET or C++ apps on Windows and need to stay on the 2022 toolset.

points.title: Who may use it for free
points.text: Individuals can build free or paid apps. Any organization can use it for classes, academic research and open source. Other non-enterprise organizations get up to five users. Enterprises, defined as more than 250 PCs or more than USD 1 million in yearly revenue, are limited to those classroom, research and open-source uses.

points.title: 2026 is now the current release
points.text: Visual Studio 2026 is the current version. Visual Studio 2022 is in extended support until January 2032, and only its latest release, 17.14, gets fixes. Community users must update to the latest release within 180 days to keep using it.

points.title: Sign-in is not required, but it nags
points.text: You can skip signing in. Microsoft notes that Community may prompt you from time to time until you sign in with a Microsoft account.

points.title: A big install on 64-bit Windows
points.text: It runs on 64-bit Windows 11, including ARM64, and Windows Server 2016 to 2025. Installs range from 850 MB to 210 GB, with 20 to 50 GB typical; 4 GB of RAM is the minimum and 16 GB is recommended. Admin rights are needed to install and update.

points.title: ARM64 leaves out some workloads
points.text: On ARM64 Windows, Python, data science, Office/SharePoint, mobile C++ and most Azure workloads are not supported. Windows 11 in S mode, Windows 10 LTSC and 32-bit Windows are not supported at all.

points.title: Many versions to roll back to
points.text: This site keeps 99 versions of the 2022 Community installer, which helps when a project is pinned to a specific 17.x build.
